evidence.quote: **Client-side encryption** – Encrypt data client-side and upload the encrypted data to Amazon S3. In this case, you manage the encryption process, the encryption keys, and related tools.

claim: Lifecycle transitions follow a waterfall model: a rule can move objects down from S3 Standard to Standard-IA, Intelligent-Tiering, One Zone-IA, Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Glacier Deep Archive, but never back up.
question: In which direction can a lifecycle rule move objects between storage classes?

values.display: waterfall model
S3 Standard storage class to the S3 Standard-IA, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, S3 One Zone-IA, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, or S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage classes

evidence.quote: Amazon S3 supports a waterfall model for transitioning between storage classes, as shown in the following diagram.
The S3 Standard storage class to the S3 Standard-IA, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, S3 One Zone-IA, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, or S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage classes.
The transition of objects to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class can go only one way.

claim: A lifecycle rule can transition objects into S3 Intelligent-Tiering; AWS suggests this when you do not know the access pattern or it changes over time.
question: Can lifecycle and Intelligent-Tiering be combined?

values.display: transition the objects to the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class for automatic cost savings

evidence.quote: When you don't know the access patterns of your objects, or if your access patterns are changing over time, you can transition the objects to the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class for automatic cost savings.

claim: By default a lifecycle configuration does not transition objects smaller than 128 KB to any storage class, because each object costs a transition request and for small objects that cost can exceed the storage saving; an object size filter can override this.
question: Why does a lifecycle rule skip small objects, and from what size?

values.display: objects smaller than 128 KB
values.spoken: objects smaller than one hundred twenty-eight kilobytes

values.display: transition costs can outweigh the storage savings

qualifiers.condition: an object size filter (ObjectSizeGreaterThan) can allow smaller objects

evidence.quote: Amazon S3 applies a default behavior to S3 Lifecycle configurations that prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned to any storage class. We don't recommend transitioning objects less than 128 KB because you are charged a transition request for each object. This means, for smaller objects, the transition costs can outweigh the storage savings.

changed.was: the default behavior allowed objects smaller than 128 KB to be transitioned only to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage classes

claim: One lifecycle rule cannot transition an object out of a storage class before that class's minimum storage duration has passed; for example, after a transition to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (90-day minimum) at day 4, the Deep Archive step must be at day 94 or later. Two separate rules can do it, but you pay the minimum-duration charge.
question: Can a single lifecycle rule move data to Glacier Instant Retrieval after 4 days and to Deep Archive after 20 days?

values.display: can't create a single Lifecycle rule that transitions objects from one storage class to another before the minimum storage duration period has passed
at least 94 days

qualifiers.condition: storage classes with a minimum storage duration

evidence.quote: You can't create a single Lifecycle rule that transitions objects from one storage class to another before the minimum storage duration period has passed.

For example, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval has a minimum storage duration of 90 days. You can't specify a lifecycle rule that transitions objects to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 4 days, and then transitions objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 20 days. In this case the S3 Glacier Deep Archive transition must occur after at least 94 days.
You can specify two rules to accomplish this, but you pay the minimum duration storage charges.

claim: If a lifecycle rule moves an object out of a class with a minimum storage duration before that duration has passed, you are charged for the rest of the duration.
question: What does it cost to transition an object out of Standard-IA or Glacier early?

values.display: charged for the remainder of that duration

qualifiers.scope: per object, storage classes with a minimum storage duration

evidence.quote: Certain storage classes have a minimum object storage duration. If you transition objects out of these storage classes before the minimum duration, you are charged for the remainder of that duration.

claim: Each object archived to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive carries 8 KB of metadata billed at S3 Standard rates plus 32 KB of index metadata billed at the Glacier class rate, so archiving many small objects adds overhead; AWS suggests aggregating small objects first.
question: Why can archiving millions of tiny objects to Glacier cost more than expected?

values.display: 8 KB of storage for the name of the object and other metadata
32 KB of storage for index and related metadata
aggregating many small objects into a smaller number of large objects

qualifiers.scope: per object archived to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive

evidence.quote: For each object archived to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive, Amazon S3 uses 8 KB of storage for the name of the object and other metadata.

For each object that is archived to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive, Amazon S3 adds 32 KB of storage for index and related metadata. This extra data is necessary to identify and restore your object. You are charged S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive rates for this additional storage.
If you are archiving small objects, consider these storage charges. Also consider aggregating many small objects into a smaller number of large objects to reduce overhead costs.

claim: A lifecycle rule can move an object in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval only to S3 Glacier Deep Archive; to put it in any other class you must restore a temporary copy and then copy the object with the new storage class.

use the restore operation to make a temporary copy of the object first

evidence.quote: Objects that are stored in the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class can only be transitioned to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class.

If you want to change the storage class of an object that is stored in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval to a storage class other than S3 Glacier Deep Archive, you must use the restore operation to make a temporary copy of the object first.

claim: Archived objects are not readable in real time: you start a restore request and wait for a temporary copy that lives for the number of days you specify; the object's storage class stays Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive.

values.display: a temporary copy of the object is available for the duration that you specify
the object's storage class remains S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive

evidence.quote: Archived objects aren't accessible in real time. You must first initiate a restore request and then wait until a temporary copy of the object is available for the duration that you specify in the request. After you receive a temporary copy of the restored object, the object's storage class remains S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

claim: Standard is the default retrieval option when a restore request names none; it typically finishes within 3–5 hours for S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and within 12 hours for S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

evidence.quote: Standard is the default option for requests that do not specify the retrieval option. Standard retrievals typically finish within 3–5 hours for the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class or S3 Intelligent-Tiering Archive Access tier. Standard retrievals typically finish within 12 hours for the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class or S3 Intelligent-Tiering Deep Archive Access tier.

claim: Bulk is the lowest-cost retrieval option: typically within 5–12 hours from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and within 48 hours from S3 Glacier Deep Archive; Bulk retrievals are free for Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Intelligent-Tiering objects.

within 48 hours
within 5–12 hours

evidence.quote: For objects stored in the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class or the S3 Intelligent-Tiering Archive Access tier, Bulk retrievals typically finish within 5–12 hours. For objects stored in the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class or the S3 Intelligent-Tiering Deep Archive Access tier, these retrievals typically finish within 48 hours. Bulk retrievals are free for objects that are stored in the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage classes.

claim: Expedited retrieval, for occasional urgent requests, typically makes objects under 250 megabytes available within 1–5 minutes from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval; it is a premium option and is not available for S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

you first need to retrieve data using the RestoreObject REST API

claim: CORS lets a web application loaded from one domain interact with S3 resources in another domain; a browser would otherwise block such JavaScript requests, and a CORS configuration on the bucket explicitly enables them per origin.
question: When does a browser upload or download to S3 need a CORS configuration on the bucket?

values.display: client web applications that are loaded in one domain to interact with resources in a different domain
A browser would normally block JavaScript from allowing those requests

qualifiers.condition: browser requests from a different origin than the bucket endpoint

evidence.quote: Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) defines a way for client web applications that are loaded in one domain to interact with resources in a different domain. With CORS support, you can build rich client-side web applications with Amazon S3 and selectively allow cross-origin access to your Amazon S3 resources.

A browser would normally block JavaScript from allowing those requests, but with CORS you can configure your bucket to explicitly enable cross-origin requests from `website.s3-website.us-east-1.amazonaws.com`.

claim: S3 uses the first CORSRule that matches a browser's preflight request: the Origin must match AllowedOrigins, the requested method must match AllowedMethods, and the requested headers must match AllowedHeaders. ACLs and policies still apply.
question: Which elements of a CORS rule must match for a browser request to be allowed?

values.display: AllowedOrigins
AllowedMethods
AllowedHeaders
The ACLs and policies continue to apply when you enable CORS on your bucket

evidence.quote: The `Origin` header in a CORS request to your bucket must match the origins in the `AllowedOrigins` element in your CORS configuration.

The HTTP methods that are specified in the `Access-Control-Request-Method` in a CORS request to your bucket must match the method or methods listed in the `AllowedMethods` element in your CORS configuration.
The headers listed in the `Access-Control-Request-Headers` header in a pre-flight request must match the headers in the `AllowedHeaders` element in your CORS configuration.
The ACLs and policies continue to apply when you enable CORS on your bucket.

claim: S3 Replication requires versioning to be enabled on both the source and the destination bucket; if you disable versioning on the destination, replication fails, and you cannot disable it on the source while a replication configuration exists.
question: What happens to replication if versioning is turned off on one of the buckets?

values.display: Both source and destination buckets must have versioning enabled
If you disable versioning on the destination bucket, replication fails
You must remove the replication configuration before you can disable versioning on the source bucket

qualifiers.scope: source and destination buckets of a replication configuration

evidence.quote: Both source and destination buckets must have versioning enabled. For more information about versioning, see [Retaining multiple versions of objects with S3 Versioning](Versioning.md).
If you attempt to disable versioning on the source bucket, Amazon S3 returns an error. You must remove the replication configuration before you can disable versioning on the source bucket.
If you disable versioning on the destination bucket, replication fails. The source object has the replication status `FAILED`.

You might choose the Region for your destination bucket based on either your business needs or cost considerations. For example, inter-Region data transfer charges vary depending on the Regions that you choose.

claim: Replication time depends on object size and can take hours for large objects; a lifecycle rule on the destination bucket counts from the object's original creation time, not from when the replica arrived.
question: When a replica lands in the destination bucket, which date does its lifecycle rule use?

values.display: the lifecycle rules honor the original creation time of the object, not when the replica became available in the destination bucket
For large objects, it can take several hours

qualifiers.scope: replicas in a destination bucket with a lifecycle configuration

evidence.quote: The time it takes for Amazon S3 to replicate an object depends on the size of the object. For large objects, it can take several hours. Although it might take a while before a replica is available in the destination, it takes the same amount of time to create the replica as it took to create the corresponding object in the source bucket. If a lifecycle configuration is enabled on a destination bucket, the lifecycle rules honor the original creation time of the object, not when the replica became available in the destination bucket.

claim: A presigned URL is a bearer token: anyone who holds it can use it, and it can do no more than the permissions of the principal who created it allow.
question: Why must a presigned URL be treated as a secret, and what limits what it can do?

values.display: presigned URLs are bearer tokens that grant access to those who possess them
limited by the permissions of the user who created it

evidence.quote: The capabilities of a presigned URL are limited by the permissions of the user who created it. In essence, presigned URLs are bearer tokens that grant access to those who possess them. As such, we recommend that you protect them appropriately.

claim: A presigned URL stops working at its configured expiration or when the credentials that signed it expire, whichever comes first; a URL signed with IAM role credentials expires when the role session ends, even if a longer expiry was set.
question: Why can a presigned URL expire before the time you set?

values.display: whichever occurs first
The presigned URL expires when the role session expires, even if you specify a longer expiration time

evidence.quote: A presigned URL expires at either its configured expiration time or when its associated credentials expire, whichever occurs first.
**IAM role credentials** – The presigned URL expires when the role session expires, even if you specify a longer expiration time.

claim: A presigned URL grants time-limited access to an object without changing the bucket policy, and can be used many times until it expires; an upload URL lets someone without AWS credentials put one specific object.

values.display: time-limited access to objects in Amazon S3 without updating your bucket policy
multiple times, up to the expiration date and time
without requiring another party to have AWS security credentials or permissions

evidence.quote: You can use presigned URLs to grant time-limited access to objects in Amazon S3 without updating your bucket policy.
You can use the presigned URL multiple times, up to the expiration date and time.
This allows an upload without requiring another party to have AWS security credentials or permissions.

claim: When someone uploads through a presigned URL, S3 creates the object in the named bucket, replaces any existing object with the same key, and the bucket owner owns the uploaded object.
question: Who owns an object uploaded with a presigned URL, and what if the key already exists?

values.display: After upload, the bucket owner will own the object
Amazon S3 replaces the existing object with the uploaded object

evidence.quote: When someone uses the URL to upload an object, Amazon S3 creates the object in the specified bucket. If an object with the same key that is specified in the presigned URL already exists in the bucket, Amazon S3 replaces the existing object with the uploaded object. After upload, the bucket owner will own the object.

claim: To restrict where presigned URLs can be used, write IAM or bucket policies with a network condition: aws:SourceIp for the public S3 endpoint, or aws:SourceVpc / aws:SourceVpce for a VPC endpoint; these restrictions apply to all S3 access, not only presigned URLs.
question: How do you stop a leaked presigned URL from working outside your network?

values.display: aws:SourceIp
aws:SourceVpc or aws:SourceVpce
These restrictions also apply outside of the presigned URL scenario

qualifiers.scope: IAM principal, bucket, or access point policies

evidence.quote: The IAM global condition key that you use depends on the type of endpoint. If you're using the public endpoint for Amazon S3, use `aws:SourceIp`. If you're using a virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint to Amazon S3, use `aws:SourceVpc` or `aws:SourceVpce`.

A network-path restriction on the IAM principal requires the user of those credentials to make requests from the specified network. A restriction on the bucket or access point requires that all requests to that resource originate from the specified network. These restrictions also apply outside of the presigned URL scenario.
